epithet.en: Queen of Argos, Murderess of the King
epithet.da: Dronning af Argos, Morderen af Kongen

3.modern-en: Clytemnestra announces the fall of Troy to the Elders, describing in vivid detail the relay of beacon fires stretching from Ida to Argos. She speaks of the victors and vanquished alike with apparent piety, warning that the gods must be honored even in conquest — though her true motives remain hidden beneath a masterful show of wifely loyalty.

5.modern-en: Clytemnestra greets the Herald with honeyed words and sends a message for Agamemnon: his faithful wife awaits him, the seal on the household unbroken. Her speech is a performance — every word designed to reassure while her real plans take shape in the shadows.

7.modern-en: Clytemnestra receives Agamemnon at the palace gates, overwhelming him with flattery and persuading him — against his better judgment — to walk on the rich purple tapestries. She then turns coolly to Cassandra, ordering her inside, and her contempt for the captive prophetess is thinly veiled.

8.modern-en: With Agamemnon inside, Clytemnestra tries to compel Cassandra to enter the palace. The prophetess's refusal reveals what the Chorus cannot yet see: Cassandra knows what awaits within. Clytemnestra withdraws with icy impatience.

10.modern-en: Clytemnestra emerges to stand over the bodies of Agamemnon and Cassandra, declaring her deed without remorse or disguise. She justifies the murder as long-overdue justice for Iphigenia's sacrifice. She and Aegisthus face down the Chorus and assert their rule over Argos.

15.modern-en: Orestes, disguised as a travelling stranger, arrives at the palace and is greeted by Clytemnestra herself. She shows him hospitality and sends word for Aegisthus. Unaware she is speaking to her own son, she plays the gracious queen — setting up the moment of recognition and doom.

17.modern-en: Clytemnestra learns that her son Orestes is dead — or so the disguised traveller claims. Her reaction seems to oscillate between grief and relief. The Nurse, who raised Orestes, does not believe her sorrow is genuine. Clytemnestra calls Aegisthus and, for an instant, clutches an axe for defense before the meeting that will end her life.

20.modern-en: The ghost of Clytemnestra rises in the underworld to rouse the sleeping Furies, demanding they pursue Orestes. She is dishonored among the dead, she cries — her own son struck her down, and the spirits of vengeance she empowered lie idle. Her ghost drives the entire machinery of the third play.

epithet.en: King of Argos, Conqueror of Troy
epithet.da: Konge af Argos, Sejrherre over Troja

2.modern-en: Agamemnon's shadow looms over the entire Parodos before he appears. The Elders recount how he sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia at Aulis so the fleet could sail to Troy — a decision the Chorus frames as both necessary and damning, the first link in a chain of violence that has not yet ended.

7.modern-en: Agamemnon returns from Troy in his chariot, with Cassandra at his side. He speaks with confidence and piety, vowing to address the city's grievances through council. Clytemnestra persuades him — against his will — to walk the purple path indoors. He acknowledges Odysseus's loyalty and enters the palace that will be his tomb.

9.modern-en: Agamemnon is heard but not seen: two offstage cries ring out as Clytemnestra strikes him in his bath. The Chorus debates helplessly whether to act.

10.modern-en: Agamemnon's body is revealed, tangled in the robe in which he was killed, lying beside Cassandra in the silver-sided laver. He is now a fixed point around which the living argue — about guilt, justice, and what comes next.

11.modern-en: Orestes stands at his father's grave-mound, offering locks of hair and prayer. Agamemnon is present only as a memory and as the reason for everything that follows — his murder is the wound the whole trilogy seeks to close.

13.modern-en: Electra and the Chorus invoke Agamemnon's spirit at the tomb, calling on him to witness his children's plea and send strength for vengeance. The libation Clytemnestra ordered, meant to placate the dead king, has instead summoned his children to act.

9.modern-en: Cassandra foretells that a son will one day return to avenge Agamemnon's death — the first mention of Orestes's purpose, spoken before the murder even occurs.

11.modern-en: Orestes returns from exile, standing at his father's grave. He has come at Apollo's command to avenge the murder, and lays a lock of hair on the tomb. When he sees the procession of mourning women, he recognizes his sister Electra among them.

13.modern-en: Orestes reveals himself to Electra at the tomb. He shows her the matching lock of hair and the robe she wove — proof of his identity. He lays out Apollo's command: avenge Agamemnon or suffer madness and divine punishment. The reunion is tender and purposeful.

14.modern-en: Orestes and Electra jointly invoke their father's spirit at the grave, appealing to Zeus and the gods to empower their vengeance. Orestes declares he will act — not only out of piety but because Apollo's oracle makes refusal impossible.

15.modern-en: Orestes plots with Electra and the Chorus: he and Pylades will arrive in disguise as Phocian travelers and request hospitality. The plan is set in motion.

17.modern-en: Disguised as a stranger, Orestes gains entry to the palace by bringing false news of his own death. He kills Aegisthus first, then confronts Clytemnestra. When she bares her breast — the breast that nursed him — he hesitates; Pylades speaks the only words he utters in the play, reminding Orestes of Apollo's command. Orestes kills his mother.

18.modern-en: Orestes stands over the bodies with the bloodied robe of Agamemnon and justifies his deed to the Chorus. But even as he speaks, his mind begins to crack: the Furies are coming for him. He flees to Delphi.

19.modern-en: Orestes is seen in the temple of Apollo at Delphi, clinging to the sacred statue, blood on his hands, surrounded by the sleeping Furies. Apollo has promised to protect him.

21.modern-en: Orestes arrives in Athens as Apollo's suppliant. He addresses Athena directly, stating his case: he acted on Apollo's orders and has been purified. He asks her to judge him.

24.modern-en: Orestes stands trial before Athena's newly constituted court, the first homicide jury in history. Apollo argues his defense; the Furies prosecute. The jury splits evenly, and Athena casts the deciding vote in Orestes's favor. He is acquitted and swears Argos's eternal friendship to Athens.

epithet.en: Daughter of Agamemnon, Princess in Exile

11.modern-en: Electra leads the slave women to Agamemnon's tomb at Clytemnestra's command, carrying libations. Orestes watches her from hiding, struck by the depth of her grief. She is conspicuous in her mourning.

13.modern-en: Electra notices the lock of hair on the tomb, matching it to Orestes. She debates with herself whether to hope — then sees him. The reunion is joyful and urgent: she has kept her loyalty to her father and her hatred of his murderers through all her years of humiliation.

14.modern-en: Electra speaks directly to her dead father at the grave, praying for rescue and vengeance. Her prayer is raw and specific: give me a purer soul than my mother's, a hand more stainless than hers. She is the moral center of this play.

15.modern-en: Electra plays no direct role in the plot that follows but her rage and loyalty have already set events in motion. The Chorus invokes her spirit as Orestes prepares to enter the palace.

epithet.en: Trojan Prophetess, Cursed to Go Unbelieved
epithet.da: Trojansk Profetinde, Forbandet til at Blive Ignoreret

7.modern-en: Cassandra arrives in Agamemnon's chariot as his war-prize from Troy. She sits silent while Clytemnestra commands her, and refuses to enter the palace — already sensing the blood and doom within its walls.

8.modern-en: Clytemnestra tries and fails to compel Cassandra. The Chorus attempts to reason with her. Cassandra remains outside, frozen in a kind of prophetic dread — she knows what waits inside, and she knows she too must enter and die.

9.modern-en: Cassandra breaks into shattering prophetic vision: she sees the children Thyestes devoured, the net of Clytemnestra, the axe that will fall. She reveals her own story — Apollo's gift of prophecy, her betrayal of him, the curse of perpetual disbelief. She removes her prophet's garlands, accepts her fate with courage, and enters the palace.

10.modern-en: Cassandra's body lies beside Agamemnon's in the silver laver. Clytemnestra calls her a rival and a harlot; the Chorus mourns her as a woman who sang her last song and met her fate. Her death is the trilogy's signal that the innocent die alongside the guilty.

Aegisthus arrives after the murder, boasting that it was the fulfillment of divine justice for the feast of Thyestes — the horror Agamemnon's father inflicted on his own. He claims intellectual authorship of the plot, though the Chorus contemptuously notes he let a woman do the killing. He and Clytemnestra assert joint rule over Argos.

15.modern-en: Aegisthus is summoned to the palace by Clytemnestra when Orestes (still disguised) brings false news of Orestes's death. He goes to hear the news — and walks into the trap Orestes has set.

17.modern-en: Aegisthus is killed offstage by Orestes. His death cry is heard; a servant rushes out to warn Clytemnestra. He dies first, before Orestes's more terrible confrontation with his mother.

epithet.en: God of Prophecy, Commander of the Vengeance

9.modern-en: Apollo stands behind Cassandra's entire story: he gave her the gift of prophecy, she refused his love, and he cursed her to speak truth that no one would believe. He is a shaping force in the first play without appearing directly.

13.modern-en: Apollo's oracle at Delphi issued the command that drives Orestes: avenge your father's murder or face madness, plague, and divine persecution. Orestes quotes the oracle's terms in full — there was no escaping it.

19.modern-en: Apollo appears in his own temple at Delphi, standing over the sleeping Furies and the suppliant Orestes. He has purified Orestes and promises to defend him. He sends him on to Athens with Hermes as guide.

21.modern-en: Apollo arrives in Athens as Orestes's advocate and witness. He bears part responsibility for the deed, he says — it was his command. He begins preparing the arguments he will deliver at trial.

24.modern-en: Apollo defends Orestes before Athena's jury, arguing that a father's blood outweighs a mother's, and that Orestes acted under divine sanction. His argument is forceful but not entirely convincing — the jury splits. Athena's vote decides it.

epithet.en: Goddess of Wisdom, Founder of the Court of Justice
epithet.da: Visdommens Gudinde, Grundlægger af Retfærdighedens Domstol

22.modern-en: Athena arrives in Athens having heard the outcry. She speaks with the Furies and with Orestes, assessing both sides. She decides the case is too grave to judge alone and announces she will convene a special court of Athenian citizens — the first jury for homicide in history.

24.modern-en: Athena presides over the trial of Orestes, calling both Apollo and the Furies to present their cases before twelve Athenian jurors. When the votes split evenly, she casts the deciding ballot for acquittal — on the principle that mercy must be available even for the most terrible acts, and that Athens will be founded on law rather than blood revenge.

26.modern-en: Athena works patiently to transform the furious Furies into the Eumenides — the Kindly Ones — by offering them a permanent honored home beneath Athens. She turns the force of ancient vengeance into a pillar of civic order. The trilogy ends with her procession.

18.modern-en: As Orestes flees after the matricide, he glimpses them approaching: the Gorgon-like spirits of his mother's blood, sent to pursue him. The Chorus sees them too. Orestes has done the commanded deed and now faces its consequence.

19.modern-en: The Furies lie coiled in sleep around Orestes in Apollo's temple at Delphi. The Pythia describes them with horror — not Gorgons exactly, but something worse. Apollo stands over them, keeping them at bay long enough for Orestes to flee to Athens.

20.modern-en: Clytemnestra's ghost rouses the sleeping Furies with stinging reproaches. They wake to find their quarry gone and rage at Apollo's interference — the ancient powers of night-justice versus the newer Olympian order.

21.modern-en: The Furies track Orestes to Athens like hounds following a blood trail. They are relentless, ancient, and explicitly not bound by the logic of reason — only by the law of blood: a mother's blood must be avenged.

22.modern-en: The Furies present their case to Athena: Orestes killed his mother. They are the guardians of that most fundamental law. They respect Athena's authority enough to agree to a trial, but warn that if they lose, they will blight the land of Athens.

23.modern-en: The Furies sing their binding-song over Orestes, invoking the power of madness and ruin that they can pour into any man who has shed kindred blood. They are not evil — they are the consequence.

24.modern-en: The Furies prosecute Orestes at trial, pressing the undeniable fact: he killed his own mother. They are outmaneuvered by Apollo's arguments but the jury is split. Athena's vote acquits Orestes, and the Furies erupt in rage at the outcome.

26.modern-en: Athena persuades the Furies to accept honors beneath Athens and transform from persecutors into protectors — the Eumenides, the Kindly Ones. They relent by degrees. The terror of the underworld becomes the foundation of civic justice. Their acceptance closes the cycle of violence.

epithet.en: Witnesses of the House of Atreus

2.modern-en: The Chorus of old Argive men opens the drama, recalling the launch of the fleet to Troy ten years ago and the sacrifice of Iphigenia at Aulis. They establish the trilogy's central themes: justice, suffering, and the inexorable law of cause and consequence.

4.modern-en: The Elders reflect on Zeus and suffering, on the curse of the house of Atreus, and on Helen as the instrument of Troy's destruction. They are uneasy — the news of victory rings hollow against a background of blood.

6.modern-en: The Elders meditate on the nature of justice and sin, and on Helen, whose beauty launched the war. They feel the shadow of doom without being able to name it — a studied helplessness that will recur when the king cries out from within.

8.modern-en: The Elders are seized with formless dread as Agamemnon enters the palace. They sense the doom they cannot prevent. Their odes carry the moral weight of the play.

10.modern-en: The Elders debate frantically when Agamemnon cries out inside. Clytemnestra reveals the bodies. The Elders condemn her, mourn their king, and warn that Orestes will return — setting the stage for the second play.

12.modern-en: The slave women carry libations to Agamemnon's tomb at Clytemnestra's fearful command — she was driven here by a nightmare. Their song mourns the house: they are captives who witnessed the murder and now carry its guilt-offerings to the grave.

13.modern-en: The Chorus counsels Electra and discovers Orestes with her. They become active conspirators in the plan for vengeance, offering advice and solidarity throughout.

15.modern-en: The Chorus rehearses a catalogue of female crimes — Althaia, Scylla, the women of Lemnos — as a dark frame for Clytemnestra's act. They cheer Orestes on and keep watch.

16.modern-en: While Orestes and Pylades are inside, the Chorus sings of terrible deeds by women through history — a meditation on what Clytemnestra represents — and steels themselves for what is about to happen.

17.modern-en: The Chorus intercepts the Nurse who is going to warn Aegisthus and persuades her to change the message — a crucial intervention that ensures Aegisthus arrives unarmed, alone, and walkable into the trap.

18.modern-en: The Chorus hails the deed done — two murders, but justice achieved. Yet they see the Furies already gathering around Orestes. Three great storms have struck the house of Atreus; the reckoning is not over.

11.modern-en: Pylades arrives with Orestes at Agamemnon's tomb. He is a silent presence in the opening scenes, accompanying his friend but saying nothing yet.

17.modern-en: Pylades speaks his one — and only — speech in the entire trilogy. When Orestes hesitates before killing Clytemnestra, unable to strike his own mother, Pylades speaks three lines: "Where then would be Apollo's oracle? Count all men your enemies rather than the gods." These three lines are the hinge of the play.

epithet.en: Sentinel on the Roof of Atreus

1.modern-en: The Watchman has spent a year on the roof of the palace of Atreus, watching for the beacon that will signal Troy's fall. When it blazes, he dances for joy — but his joy is laced with unease. He knows something is wrong in the house below him and can say nothing: "An ox stands heavy on my tongue." He is the prologue's conscience.

epithet.en: Returned Soldier, Bearer of News from Troy

5.modern-en: The Herald returns from Troy, overjoyed to be home after ten years of war and suffering. He brings news of victory and of Agamemnon's imminent arrival, but must admit that Menelaus and the fleet were scattered in a storm. He is honest, weary, and oblivious to the doom that awaits his king inside the palace.

19.modern-en: The Pythia opens the third play with a pious prayer naming the succession of divine owners of the oracle at Delphi. She enters the temple — and staggers back out in horror. She has seen Orestes at the sacred navel-stone, surrounded by the monstrous Furies. Her terror is the audience's first sight of what pursues him.

17.modern-en: The Nurse rushes from the palace to bring Aegisthus the news that Orestes is dead. She is grief-stricken — she raised the boy herself, tended him as an infant, and believes the report. The Chorus intercepts her and changes her message, ensuring Aegisthus arrives without his guards. Her genuine love for Orestes, and her grief, is the most human moment in a play of terrible purpose.
